title: KV-cache pressure and memory-fabric comparison across A100/H100/L40S
body:
Summary:

This note captures a set of ad-hoc benchmarks we ran to understand how KV-cache pressure interacts with memory fabric (HBM vs. host DRAM) and interconnect characteristics across representative cloud SKUs of A100, H100 and L40S. The motivating observation from customer incidents and our tail-latency alarms was that p99 latency spikes correlate with long-context sessions even when average token throughput is low. We suspect cross-sku differences (driver/CUDA, NVLink topology, PCIe lanes, host memory behavior) amplify KV-cache thrashing and cause unexpected stalls.

Goals:
- Measure throughput and tail latency with increasing KV-cache working set (simulated long contexts) across SKUs and driver/CUDA combos.
- Identify whether stalls are compute-bound, memory-bandwidth bound (HBM), or interconnect/backpressure related.
- Produce concrete mitigations or scheduler heuristics to avoid high p99s (e.g., KV-cache eviction thresholds, routing to smaller-seq models or pinned model variants).

Experimental matrix (high level):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (single-socket), H100 80GB, L40S 48GB
- Cloud SKUs tested: aws-p4d (A100), gcp-a2-megagpu (A100 variant), azure-nc24s-v3 (A100), aws-trn1/h100-equivalent on gcp (H100), azure-l40s (L40S) — note: variety kept to exercise different NVLink/PCIe configs
- Driver/CUDA: NVIDIA driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, driver 535 + CUDA 12.1, driver 545 + CUDA 12.2 where available
- Context lengths: 512, 2048, 8192, 32k simulated via KV-cache growth
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 (to see interaction with batching and continuous batching logic)
- Workload: decoder-only 30B-ish model (quantized fp16 where applicable) with KV-cache instrumentation enabled in runtime
- Measurement points: tokens/sec (steady-state), p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU memory utilization (HBM), host pinned memory, PCIe read/write counters (where driver exposes), PCIe saturation (ethtool/nvml proxies), kernel context switch rates on host

Setup details (commands / config snippets):
- Runtime: branch bench/kv-pressure-experiments from serving-runtime repo (PR GH#3124). Built with profiling hooks enabled.
- Launch: docker run --gpus all --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE ...; using the same container to avoid host image variance.
- Prometheus metrics collected from runtime: tokens_out_total, batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_evictions_total, kv_cache_size_bytes, hbm_used_bytes, host_pinned_mem_bytes, cuda_context_time_ms.
- nvml sampling script: sample_nvml.py (attached to linked artifacts) polled at 200ms.

Key results (condensed):
- Small contexts (<=2048): all SKUs behaved similarly for batch=1. Throughput differences were within expected model variance. p99 stable < 2x p50.
- Mid contexts (2048-8192): A100 SKUs showed increased variance in p99 only on some driver versions (525/11.8) — we saw occasional p99 spikes that correlated with host pinned memory growth and a flurry of KV-cache evictions on the runtime. H100 and L40S showed fewer spikes but higher steady HBM usage.
- Large contexts (32k simulated KV): A100 (multi-socket/NGC setups with certain cloud images) experienced repeated stalls with p99 > 10s in worst cases. H100 exhibited increased overall latency but fewer multi-second stalls. L40S was interesting: HBM saturated earlier (smaller device HBM), triggering host pinned memory fallbacks; this caused sustained higher p95 but fewer extreme p99 tails.

Representative table (aggregated numbers, batch=1, driver=535/CUDA12.1):
- A100 (aws-p4d): tokens/sec steady ~1.0k at 8k context, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~1.9s (with 3/50 runs >5s due to eviction storms)
- H100 (gcp-h100): tokens/sec steady ~1.2k at 8k context, p95 ~360ms, p99 ~900ms (rare >2s)
- L40S (azure-l40s): tokens/sec steady ~0.9k at 8k context, p95 ~560ms, p99 ~1.1s (consistent, fewer outliers)

Observations and hypotheses:
1) KV-cache eviction storms are tightly linked to host pinned memory behavior when HBM available is exceeded. On some cloud images, driver behavior caused a delayed fallback/transfer that blocks the inference thread — this shows up as multi-second p99 spikes.
2) Driver + CUDA combination matters: older driver/CUDA (525+11.8) on some A100 AMIs had less efficient page migration and higher PCIe stall times for big transfers. Newer drivers (535/545 families) improved migration behavior in our tests.
3) H100's larger HBM and NVLink topology reduces frequency of eviction but when it happens, the transfer cost is larger — but the runtime overlaps transfers better on our H100 infra so stalls less often.
4) L40S has less HBM and causes earlier host fallback; however its swap pattern is steadier (more frequent small transfers) which leads to higher median but fewer multi-second pauses.
5) Batching changes the dynamics: larger batch sizes amortize KV transfer overhead (fewer context switches) so p99 improves relative to batch=1 until you hit HBM capacity where batching amplifies stall depth.

Root-cause investigations (notes):
- nvml PCIe counters + driver traces indicate that eviction-related host transfers are serialized with compute launches in older drivers on A100 cloud images. We captured timestamps where a cudaMemcpy triggered a 100–500ms window with no kernels scheduled.
- strace / perf on host shows increased io-wait and page-fault related syscalls near p99 spikes, consistent with pinned memory migration overhead.
- We observed different kernel versions and iommu settings in the cloud images — some provider images have IOMMU on by default which can change DMA behavior.

Immediate mitigations we tried (and results):
- Aggressive KV-cache trimming: limiting per-request KV growth capped p99 spikes at expense of slight quality regressions. Useful as emergency fallback.
- Prefetching hottest KV pages in background as streaming arrives: reduced eviction storms by ~60% in our H100 runs (needs tuning to avoid extra memory pressure).
- Driver upgrade test: moving from 525->535 reduced frequency of >2s stalls on A100 by ~70% in our sample; recommend validating images before scaling.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of the behavior is provider-image specific (kernel/IOMMU/BIOS) vs. the GPU driver version? We need a controlled bare-metal test to separate effects.
- Can runtime overlap be improved further? Our profiler shows some overlap but still serialized transfers in worst cases.
- Are there CPU-side scheduling knobs (isolcpus, disabling frequency governors) that consistently reduce page migration delays?

Suggested next experiments (prioritized):
1) Bare-metal isolated node (same GPU models) with matched driver versions to separate cloud image variance. Compare with cloud images that show worst behavior. Owner: Marek. ETA: 2 weeks.
2) Instrumented run with per-GPU page migration tracing (using CUDA memprof where possible) to capture exact migration sizes and timing. Owner: Aisha. ETA: 1 week.
3) Scheduler change experiment: test runtime patch that pre-emptively pins and stages KV blocks into a reserved HBM window before they are needed, controlled by policy. Measure p99 impact and memory overhead. Owner: Jonah. ETA: 3 weeks (prototype).

Action items (short):
- Validate driver 535+ on all A100 AMIs used in Hosted and Dedicated fleets. (Infra & Release Eng)
- Add a KV-cache eviction threshold heuristic that triggers a graceful fallback to smaller model variant instead of allowing eviction storms. (Runtime team)
- Add a diagnostic trace flag that records host pinned mem allocations and GPU transfer windows into our request traces for easier root-cause mapping. (Observability)

Notes to self / rough logs: 
- 2026-02-20: first runaway p99 observed on aws-p4d with 525 drivers; reproduced locally on similar AMI.
- 2026-02-25: driver 535 trial reduced extreme tails but increased steady p95 slightly.
- 2026-03-03: prototyped prefetcher, promising on H100 but needs an eviction-aware controller.

References / links:
- internal playbook: https://redwood-confluence/internal/serving-runtime/kv-cache-playbook
- experiment code PR: GH#3124
- related incident: JIRA-8791

Conclusion:
The behavior is multi-factor: HBM capacity, driver/CUDA version, cloud image kernel/IOMMU settings, and our runtime eviction policies all interplay to produce the observed tails. Short-term wins are validating drivers and introducing conservative runtime fallbacks. Medium-term work should focus on better prefetching and overlapping strategies plus a bare-metal campaign to isolate provider-image variables.

Unresolved items are flagged in JIRA-8791 and linked in GH#3124. Feedback welcome — this is a rough working doc (notes + numbers) aimed at prioritizing infra + runtime fixes.
